claims.text: Adding 1–2 at.% yttrium during melting and subsequent processing will promote in situ formation of Y2O3 nanoparticles.
The resulting Y2O3 nanoparticles will be finely and uniformly dispersed in the refractory-HEA matrix.
Y2O3 particles will obstruct grain-boundary sliding at high temperature.
Y2O3 particles will resist dislocation climb at high temperature.
Obstructing grain-boundary sliding and dislocation climb will increase the alloy's creep resistance.
The limited oxide volume fraction will prevent an appreciable increase in alloy density.
The limited oxide volume fraction will preserve room-temperature ductility.
At approximately 1000°C under sustained creep or stress loading, the Y-added alloy will have 20–30% better creep resistance than the Y-free baseline.
The Y-added alloy will exhibit no measurable loss of room-temperature mechanical performance relative to the baseline.
The intervention is expected to work only when it produces a uniform nanoscale oxide dispersion rather than large agglomerates.
Keeping the yttrium addition within 1–2 at.% will avoid significant density changes.
Keeping the yttrium addition within 1–2 at.% will avoid deleterious effects on low-temperature ductility.
The optimal yttrium content and the magnitude of improvement depend on oxide-particle size distribution and processing conditions.
A Y-added sample and a Y-free control processed under identical conditions can test the intervention.
Failure to obtain at least a 20% improvement in creep resistance at 1000°C would falsify the predicted high-temperature benefit.
